passed.title: Division by zero yields inf/NaN, not null or an error
passed.trap: `Expr.truediv` (and the `/` operator) follows IEEE-754. `n/0` gives `±inf` and `0/0` gives `NaN`. It does not return null as SQL `NULLIF` code expects, and it does not raise. Because `NaN` is not null, a later `Expr.fill_null` or `Expr.is_null` misses these rows, and they silently poison sums and means. Integer inputs also come back as `Float64`. Guard the denominator explicitly with `pl.when(...).then(None).otherwise(...)`, or clean up afterwards with `Expr.fill_nan` and `Expr.is_infinite`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"x": [1, 0, 4], "y": [0, 0, 2]})
out = df.with_columns(
    naive=pl.col("x").truediv(pl.col("y")),
    safe=pl.when(pl.col("y") == 0)
    .then(None)
    .otherwise(pl.col("x").truediv(pl.col("y"))),
)
print(out)
print(out.select(
    pl.col("naive").is_null().sum().alias("naive_nulls"),
    pl.col("naive").fill_null(0).sum().alias("naive_sum_after_fill_null"),
    pl.col("safe").is_null().sum().alias("safe_nulls"),
    pl.col("safe").fill_null(0).sum().alias("safe_sum"),
))

passed.title: Expr.slice takes (offset, length), not (start, end)
passed.trap: `Expr.slice(offset, length)` uses a length as its second argument, not an exclusive end index like Python `[1:3]` or pandas `iloc[1:3]`. Writing `slice(1, 3)` while expecting rows 1 and 2 returns three rows instead. If you think in start/end terms, pass `end - start` as the length. Leaving `length=None` takes everything from `offset` onward.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]})
# Python-style intent: rows [1:3] -> 20, 30
wrong = df.select(pl.col("a").slice(1, 3))
start, end = 1, 3
right = df.select(pl.col("a").slice(start, end - start))
print(wrong["a"].to_list())
print(right["a"].to_list())

passed.title: Expr.std defaults to sample std (ddof=1), not population std
passed.trap: `Expr.std` divides by `N - ddof` with `ddof=1` by default, which gives the sample standard deviation. Code ported from NumPy (where `np.std` defaults to population, ddof=0), or written with a population formula in mind, will silently get a larger value. Pass `ddof=0` explicitly when you need the population standard deviation.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]})
print(df.select(
    pl.col("a").std().alias("default_ddof1"),
    pl.col("a").std(ddof=0).alias("population_ddof0"),
))
